title: How rape allegations at Cornell test the college, prosecutors, and media
text:
How rape allegations at Cornell test the college, prosecutors, and media
Prosecutors, college administrators, and the media are working in parallel around the alleged sexual assault at Cornell University.
Two years after a Cornell University student reported a sexual assault at a fraternity house, the case is now in the public spotlight after she filed a lawsuit that prompted the reopening of a criminal investigation. At the same time, a national debate over the case’s handling and what constitutes consent is playing out. It has sparked a viral campaign on social media where people are declaring “I am Jane Doe” in solidarity with the former student and in response to people who are trying to publicly identify her.
The Cornell University case is one in a long line of college rape allegations to surge into national headlines in recent years. When these allegations become big national news, three separate systems scramble: the university, the criminal justice system, and the media, which include traditional news outlets and now increasingly social media influencers. All three move at different speeds, use different standards, and, sometimes, can lead people to reach different conclusions.
Cornell has agreed to an independent review on how university officials handled the allegations. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has appointed the state attorney general, Letitia James, as special prosecutor. Media coverage is helping to shape public response.
The alleged sexual assault at Cornell University has drawn national attention. The different roles that colleges, the criminal justice system, and media play in such cases are not always clear.
Here’s a look at how these cases are handled and some of the inherent challenges.
How do universities respond to assault reports?
Details of the alleged sexual assault have emerged in recent days, in part from a police interview transcript from November 2024, less than a month after the incident. The female student described herself as “incapacitated” in a situation that involved alcohol, drugs, and a sexual encounter that escalated as more men entered the fraternity house room. “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped,” she reported to police.
Cornell’s handling of the 2024 complaint has drawn sharp public criticism. The university says some of the seven accused students were expelled and others were temporarily suspended following its investigation at the time. Writing essays was not the sole consequence for any of those involved, according to the university.
Under Title IX, the federal law prohibiting sex-based discrimination in education programs, students can report misconduct to their school, to police, to both, or to neither. Schools must help students who choose to go to law enforcement.
Universities must investigate “fairly, thoroughly, and transparently, while protecting the rights of everyone involved,” says Songyon Shin, an assistant professor of criminal justice at Nevada State University. Best practices include responding immediately, offering support, preserving evidence, explaining options clearly, and investigating impartially. But universities juggle competing interests, she says via email, and “institutional, structural, or contextual factors” can sometimes shape outcomes.
Kristen Jozkowski, a sexual health professor at Indiana University, who studies sexual consent, says some of Cornell’s response matches best practices.
“The university is not the criminal justice system, so expelling them is the harshest penalty that could be implemented,” she says.
She noted that universities answer to many stakeholders, including administrators and influential alumni, as well as well-funded fraternities and athletic programs, some with histories of mishandled misconduct cases.
Separate from the school’s required investigation is the criminal investigation. The student reported the incident to campus police.
What challenges do prosecutors face in cases like this?
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who originally considered the case, has said he only saw a campus police summary of the young woman’s statement, not the transcript of her full interview with police, before deciding not to pursue criminal charges. Cornell says more information was provided.
On Friday, Governor Hochul questioned that decision. “In what world does the district attorney not even interview her, or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?”
The case’s newfound attention began Sept. 16, when Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit seeking a jury trial against defendants, including Cornell University, the Chi Phi fraternity, seven of its members, and her sorority, Delta Delta Delta, among others.
On Monday, Mr. Van Houten said he was reopening the criminal investigation. But on Thursday night, Governor Hochul said she had lost faith in his “ability to fairly oversee it.” Attorney General James said during a news conference Friday, “We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses, and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions.”
In campus cases involving drugs or alcohol, and acquaintances, prosecutors examine every interaction during the relevant period, says Dan Schorr, a former New York sex crimes prosecutor who now investigates misconduct cases for schools. “Who were they messaging? Who were they interacting with? What alcohol or drugs did they consume? How are they acting that might be consistent or inconsistent with incapacitation?”
A thorough investigation by prosecutors is critical before reaching a decision about whether to take evidence to a grand jury, says Deborah Tuerkheimer, a law professor at Northwestern University. “Being informed by an understanding of trauma and how it impacts memory and narration, I think, is really helpful.”
After a traumatic experience, the victim might relay a “truthful account that may evolve,” suggests Ms. Tuerkheimer.
Chief among challenges in sexual assault cases is “an undue tendency to doubt or blame or dismiss accusers,” Ms. Tuerkheimer says. Others can include delays in reporting and a lack of independent witnesses.
A prosecutor then tries to sort through any corroborative evidence.
A grand jury would review evidence from prosecutors and decide whether to indict. If it does, there’s still no guarantee a jury trial would lead to a conviction. If the grand jury were to find the evidence insufficient, there would be no criminal case.
Despite national attention, experts say, public pressure should not determine whether charges are brought. No one has been charged in this case.
How can media coverage shape these cases?
Media covering the Cornell case need a clear journalistic purpose, says Kelly McBride, senior vice president of the Poynter Institute and chair of the Craig Newmark Center for Ethics and Leadership. Without it, the media add to the noise instead of serving their audience.
One of the biggest challenges facing media outlets is that public interest in such stories pushes newsrooms to produce a lot of stories. Without a defined purpose, journalists end up repeating what others report, including information that might be flawed, Ms. McBride says.
In turn, intense news coverage has multilayered effects. While coverage can put pressure on the justice system to act and serve as a release valve for widespread frustration, she says, it can make it harder for investigators to gather clean evidence.
Defense attorneys argue that it might complicate jury selection, says Kathleen Bartzen Culver, director of the Center for Journalism Ethics at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.
“Anytime anything becomes sensational in traditional news or viral in social media platforms, you have to become concerned of the fair-trial rights of anyone who is accused,” she says.
Adding to the Cornell allegations is the social media influencer clamor, Ms. Culver says. Compared with past cases and the #MeToo movement, direct-to-camera influencer videos have created a new level of intensity. That content mostly isn’t journalism, Ms. McBride says, but readers scrolling their feeds rarely distinguish influencers from news outlets.
Frequently, news outlets stop following the story soon after the initial alarming report, says Bruce Shapiro, executive director of the Global Center for Journalism and Trauma.
“Too often, local newsrooms don’t have resources to follow up systematically on sexual assault cases,” Mr. Shapiro says. “What about the next phase? What does the investigation look like? What does healing for survivors look like?
“The story doesn’t end with an arrest or even a conviction,” he says. “We are doing a disservice if we only focus on the act of violence and not following up.”
